saint.name: St. Catherine of Siena
saint.summary: On the morning a young man was to be beheaded in Siena, a dyer’s daughter went ahead of him to the block and stretched her own neck on it while she waited. When he came, he laughed to see her and said nothing but “Jesus” and “Catherine,” and she received his head into her hands. As a girl, Catherine of Siena had asked for nothing but a small room and silence. Then she was sent out, to plague wards, to the pope at Avignon, to a city in revolt, and to a Church split between two popes. Did she lose the silence, or carry it with her?
saint.biography:
“I Have Received a Head”

In a prison in Siena, sometime in the middle of the 1370s, a young nobleman of Perugia named Niccolò di Toldo was waiting to die. He had been condemned for rash words spoken against the government of the city, and he did not take the sentence quietly. He raged in his cell, and he refused to make his confession. Then a woman of Siena began to visit him, a dyer’s daughter with no office in the Church and no rank in the city, and the raging stopped.

She talked to him about the death that was coming as if it were a feast. “Take comfort, my sweet brother,” she told him, “for soon we shall come to the wedding. You will go to it bathed in the sweet blood of the Son of God, with the sweet name of Jesus.” Then she made him a promise: “I will wait for you at the place of justice.” The young man who had raged in his cell could hardly take it in. Where did such grace come to him from, he asked, that the sweetness of his soul would be waiting for him at the sacred place of justice? It would seem a thousand years, he said, until he got there. Before the end he rested his head on her breast. She felt, she wrote afterward, a jubilation and the scent of his blood, “and it was not without the scent of my own, which I long to shed for my sweet spouse Jesus.”

Early on the last morning she went to him again, and he heard Mass and received Communion. Then she went ahead to the place of justice to wait for him, as she had promised. While she waited, she lay down and stretched her own neck on the block. Then he came.

“Then he came, like a gentle lamb, and seeing me he began to laugh, and he wanted me to make the sign of the cross over him. … His mouth said nothing but ‘Jesus’ and ‘Catherine.’ And as he said it, I received his head into my hands, fixing my eye on the divine goodness and saying, ‘I will.’”

— Catherine of Siena, letter to Raymond of Capua, Tommaseo no. CCLXXIII (our translation from the Italian)

Fra Tommaso Caffarini, a Dominican who had followed her since he was a youth, was there, and he wrote later that it had all happened “in presenzia mia,” in my presence. A great multitude of people had come to watch, he remembered, but she told her confessor and her friends afterward that she had seen no one at all. She wrote the whole story to that confessor, Raymond of Capua, who was away from Siena. The letter begins with a shout: “Up, up, sweetest my father! and let us sleep no more! … I have just received a Head in my hands.”

The woman with the head in her hands was Caterina Benincasa, known to the world as Catherine of Siena. In the few years left to her she would stand before a pope at Avignon and urge him home to Rome. She would write to a queen, scold the government of Florence, and stay on in that city through a revolt in which the mob put her own life in danger. And she would dictate a book of such teaching that, six centuries later, Pope Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church. She did all of it as a laywoman, and she dictated her letters to friends who wrote them down for her.

Yet as a girl she had asked for almost nothing except a small room and silence. For three years she spoke to no one but her confessor and left the house only for Mass. How did that girl come to the scaffold, the papal court, and the center of the Church’s troubles in her century? And when the world finally had her, did she lose the God she had found in the silence? The answer begins in a crowded house in Fontebranda, where one day her family would take her room away from her.

The Dyer’s Daughter of Fontebranda

Catherine’s father, Jacomo di Benincasa, was a dyer in the Fontebranda district of Siena. His wife, Lapa di Puccio di Piagente, bore him so many children that Raymond of Capua, who later wrote Catherine’s life, counted twenty-five. Catherine was one of the youngest. She was born a twin, but her twin sister, Giovanna, died soon after birth, and when another baby girl came later, the family gave her the same name. The traditional year of Catherine’s birth is 1347, on the eve of the great plague. Lapa nursed this child at her own breast, Caffarini wrote, and loved her above all the others.

She grew into a child so full of gladness that people called her Eufrosina for the joy she gave them. At five she would kneel on every step of the stairs of her house to greet the Virgin Mary. On those same stairs, Caffarini claimed, she sometimes seemed to be carried down through the air without touching the steps at all.

When she was about six, she was walking along the lane called Vallepiatta with her brother Stefano, on the way home from their married sister Bonaventura’s house. In the sky above the church of the Dominican friars she saw Christ seated on a throne. He was dressed as a pope, in the robes and the tiara of the Supreme Pontiff, and with him stood the apostles Peter, Paul, and John. He looked at her and blessed her. She stood there, held by what she saw, until Stefano pulled at her hand to bring her back. The child would spend her last years fighting for the men who wore those robes.

Not long afterward, by Caffarini’s account, she set out to become a hermit. At six or seven she tucked a single loaf of bread into the front of her dress and walked out of the city toward what Caffarini calls the desert of the Fathers. Outside the walls she found a cave, or perhaps an old cellar, and went in to pray. There, Caffarini writes, she was lifted from the ground and remained in prayer until the ninth hour, the middle of the afternoon. Then she understood that this was not God’s will for her, and she found herself back at the city gate. She told no one where she had been, and her mother assumed she had spent the day at Bonaventura’s.

The little hermit had another secret. By her own later account, she was seven when she promised Christ that she would belong to him alone and never marry. Her family, meanwhile, had other plans for her, and when she was about twelve they began to put them into effect.

A Cell No One Could Take

The first to move against the promise was her sister. At Lapa’s urging, Bonaventura persuaded Catherine to dye her hair and to dress herself up like any other girl of marriageable age. Catherine went along with it for a while, and years later she still grieved over it and wept over it as a sin. Then, in August 1362, Bonaventura died, and Catherine went back to her old austerity.

The family pressed on with the marriage anyway. Catherine turned for help to Fra Tommaso della Fonte, a Dominican friar who was a relative and had become her first confessor. He told her to cut off her hair. She did, and her family answered in kind. They took away her room, and they set her to the work of a servant in her own house.

Catherine answered with an idea she would live by for the rest of her life. If she could not have a cell of stone, she would build one inside herself. Raymond describes how she made a cell in her own mind and resolved never to leave it, whatever her hands were doing. And she changed the way she saw the people who were punishing her. She would serve her father as if he were Christ, her mother as if she were the Virgin Mary, and her brothers as if they were the apostles. The servant’s work they had given her as a punishment became, in her mind, the service of Christ’s own household.

Around this time she dreamed of St. Dominic, the founder of the Order of Preachers. In the dream he offered her a lily and the habit of the women penitents of his order. The battle at home ended in an unexpected way. One day her father came into Stefano’s room and found her kneeling there in prayer, with a white dove above her head. From then on Jacomo would not let anyone stand in her way: his daughter was free to serve God.

Catherine knew exactly what she wanted next. She asked for the habit she had seen in her dream.

Three Years Without a Word

The habit belonged to the Mantellate, the Sisters of Penance of St. Dominic. They were not enclosed nuns, and Catherine would wear the habit in her father’s house. In Raymond’s telling, the Mantellate of Siena were all widows, and at first they refused to take a young girl. They changed their minds only when Catherine fell ill and the illness left her so disfigured that no one could worry any longer about her beauty. She received the habit, probably early in 1363, when she was about sixteen.

Once Lapa took Catherine to the hot baths at Vignone, and there Catherine scalded herself in the boiling water, thinking of the fire of hell. She once said that she would stand over the mouth of hell herself and close it.

Then she shut herself into her cell at home, and for three years she lived there in silence. She spoke to no one except her confessor, and she left the house only to go to Mass. Her fasting grew so severe that her confessor ordered her to eat; when she obeyed, she chewed the food and spat it out without swallowing. Raymond later wrote that in the years when he was a witness of her life, she lived without taking any food or drink as nourishment. Physicians who were brought to her, he said, admitted it was beyond nature. He added a warning that readers should not try to copy her. Not everyone believed it. Some in her own lifetime, among them men respected for their spiritual life, said she was not fasting at all but eating very well in secret.

In those years, by Raymond’s account, she learned to read without a teacher. And she learned the lesson that would sit at the center of everything she later taught. Raymond records it as a single sentence that Christ spoke to her.

“Thou art she who art not, and I am He who am.”

— Christ to Catherine, in Raymond of Capua’s Legenda Maior (Gardner’s English, 1907)

It sounds harsh, but she heard it as the key to everything. To know her own nothingness, she would later dictate in her book, was the way to know better the goodness of God toward her. Whatever was good in her came from him.

The silence was not peaceful all the way through. Near the end of the three years, Raymond writes, she suffered an assault by demons. When it was over, Christ showed himself to her on the cross, and his words to her were simple: “I was in thy heart.”

On the last day of carnival, the eve of Lent, probably in 1366, Christ came to her. In Raymond’s account the Virgin Mary took Catherine’s hand and held it out to her Son, while King David played on a psaltery. Christ placed on her finger a ring of gold set with four pearls and a diamond, and took her as his bride. She said afterward that she could always see the ring on her hand, though no one else ever could. The years of the closed door were almost over. Soon the girl who had spoken to no one would have a household of followers, and enemies among her own sisters.

A Heart Taken, a Heart Given

In July 1370, after receiving Communion, Catherine felt Christ open her side and take her heart away. She told her confessor afterward that she had no heart any longer. He laughed at her, Raymond writes, but she insisted that she was living without one. Two days later, when she was alone in the chapel of the Dominican church in Siena, a light surrounded her, and Christ appeared with a heart that was red and shining.

“Behold, dearest daughter: as the other day I took your heart from you, so now I give you mine, that you may live by it always.”

— Christ to Catherine, in Raymond of Capua, Legenda Maior II §180 (our translation from the Latin)

A scar remained on her side at the place, Raymond reports. Her companions told him and many others that they had seen it, and when he asked her about it, she said it was so. From then on she could no longer pray, as she always had, “Lord, I commend my heart to you.” Instead she prayed, “I give you your heart.”

In those same months, in Raymond’s account, she was told that she must go out into the world. Could the cell inside her go with her? People had already begun to gather around her. Among the first were women of Siena: Alessa Saracini, Cecca Gori, and Lisa, the wife of her brother. Then came Tommaso Caffarini, about seventeen years old, and Bartolommeo di Domenico, a Dominican friar, both of whom would testify about her years later. Bartolommeo swore that in her presence all carnal passion died away, and that she was always joyful and merry of face.

The people she drew were not all devout. Andrea di Naddino Bellanti was known in Siena as a blasphemer. Francesco Saracini was a nobleman of eighty. Jacomo Tolomei had killed two men, and after he met Catherine he was changed, it was said, “from wolf to lamb, from lion to watch-dog.” At such moments of victory she would laugh and cry out, “Love, Love, I have conquered Thee with Thyself.”

Some of the stories told about her in these years have a smile in them. There was a cask of wine, the story went, that would not run dry however much was drawn from it. When people began to talk about it, Catherine begged God to turn the wine to dregs so that the talk would stop, and the wine turned to sediment. The Florentine Miracoli tell of a beggar to whom she gave her tunic, and who was Christ. At Montepulciano, the Miracoli and Raymond both say, she bent to kiss the foot of St. Agnes, and the foot rose to meet her lips. Meanwhile her body seemed to live on less and less. From the autumn of 1372 eating grew harder for her month by month, and in 1373, from Passion Sunday to the Ascension, her friends said, she took nothing for fifty-five days but Holy Communion.

Not everyone in Siena was pleased. Some of her own sisters among the Mantellate, and some of the friars, spoke against her. Once, when she was rapt in ecstasy at prayer, they threw her out of the church. One friar kicked her as she lay there. Another pricked her with a needle; she felt nothing until she came to herself, and then she felt the pain. Someone told her that people were calling her a hypocrite. She did not argue. “They speak sooth,” she answered, “for, if the world knew me, it would stone me.”

One story of how she treated an enemy is hard to read even now. A sister who had slandered her, Caffarini writes, fell ill with a cancer, and Catherine nursed her. One day, as she dressed the sore, the smell turned her stomach. “You will take into yourself what so displeases you,” she told her own body, and she drank the matter from the bowl. Afterward she said she had never tasted a drink so perfect in taste and scent. That night, in Caffarini’s telling, Christ drew her mouth to the wound in his side and said, “Drink, most loving daughter, from my side.” The writer of the Miracoli knew a form of the story as early as 1374.

In the spring of 1374 the Dominican friars, gathered in Florence for their general chapter, summoned her to appear before them.

Plague Summer in Siena

Catherine came to Florence in May 1374 with three women companions who kept watch over her, and she stayed until 29 June. Her visit had a result no one planned. A Florentine layman who heard about her began to write down the wonders told of her. He finished his little book, the Miracoli, on 10 October 1374, while she was still alive and only twenty-seven by its reckoning.

By then she was back in Siena, and the plague had come to the city. Catherine and her companions went to nurse the sick. With her went Raymond of Capua, the Dominican friar who became her confessor and, after her death, her biographer. Every day the two of them visited the wards where the dying lay. In her own family she buried eight nephews, and the Florentine writer of the Miracoli noted the joy with which she did it.

One morning Raymond learned that Matteo di Cenni, the rector of the Misericordia hospital, had fallen sick in the night. The physician who examined him found the evident signs of the pestilence, with the fever and the swelling in the groin. Raymond went to find Catherine and pleaded with her: “O mother, will you suffer this good man … to die after this sort?” Her answer sounded almost like a rebuke. “Do you take me to be a God,” she said, “that you would have me deliver a mortal man from death?” Then, Raymond remembered, she smiled and promised.

She went to Matteo, and from the street outside she called to him: “Rise, Master Matthew, rise; this is no time to lie softly in bed.” The fever left him at once, and so did the swelling. That same morning, Raymond recalled, they sat down and ate a meal of raw onions together.

Another victim, a hermit named Fra Santi, was carried into the Misericordia, and Catherine nursed him herself. Caffarini gives the words she spoke to the dying man, as if to his soul: “I command you, blessed soul, … not to pass away now.” He recovered. Then it was Catherine’s turn: on 15 August, the Miracoli says, she nearly died. She recovered, and the next spring she went to Pisa.

Five Rays at Santa Cristina

Catherine was in Pisa in the spring of 1375 to preach the crusade, as Pope Paul VI later wrote. Two learned men of Pisa, Giovanni Gutalebraccia and Pietro Albizzi, came to test her with questions. A young novice named Giovanni Dominici, who would one day be a cardinal, watched her speak with sinners there and later wrote about it.

She had already been marked once in secret. Some time before, by her own account to Raymond, Christ had offered her a nail and pressed it into the palm of her right hand, so that the hand felt pierced through. Nothing could be seen. “I already have his stigmata in my right hand,” she told Raymond. “Though it is invisible, I can feel it, and it pains me without ceasing.”

On the fourth Sunday of Lent, 1 April 1375, Raymond said Mass in the church of Santa Cristina in Pisa, and Catherine received Communion and remained on her knees in prayer. Raymond and the others with her watched as she rose up on her knees and stretched out her arms, her face glowing. Then she fell to the floor as though she had received a mortal wound. Afterward she called Raymond to her and spoke quietly: “Know, Father, that by his mercy I now carry in my body the stigmata of the Lord Jesus.”

She told him what she had seen. The crucified Lord came down toward her in a great light, and from the five wounds of his body five blood-red rays came toward her hands, her feet, and her heart. She begged him that the marks should not appear outwardly. As she prayed, the rays turned to light, and in the form of pure light they reached her hands, her feet, and her heart. No one saw any wound on her. But the pain was real, and she did not hide it from her confessor.

“I feel in those five places, but specially in my heart, so great and violent a pain, that unless Almighty God be pleased to work a new miracle, I cannot live.”

— Catherine to Raymond of Capua, Pisa, 1 April 1375, from the old English version of Raymond’s Life (Drane, 1887)

A week later, on the following Sunday, after Communion in the same church, the pain was eased, and she told Raymond that it now strengthened her. The crucifix from whose wounds she had seen the rays come, a painted cross by Giunta Pisano, stayed in Pisa for nearly two centuries. In 1563 it was carried to Siena by night, under armed guard.

That same year she sailed to the island of Gorgona, where Carthusian monks lived under their prior, Bartolommeo Serafini, and there for the first time in her life she saw the sea. One of the young monks had been tempted to take his own life. The prior later told how Catherine’s mantle touched him, and the temptation left him. Three years later the same prior would write to her about a new pope.

The quarrels of Italy, meanwhile, were closing in around her. Florence was at odds with the pope, and Catherine had begun to write to him directly.

“Come, Come, Come”

The pope was Gregory XI, and he lived at Avignon, far from Rome. Catherine wrote to him as she wrote to everyone. Her letters usually opened with words like these: “I Catherine, servant and slave of the servants of Jesus Christ, write to you in His precious Blood.” They often ended with “sweet Jesus, Jesus Love.” In between, she called the Vicar of Christ “Babbo,” Daddy, and she told him exactly what she thought.

“Oh me, oh me, sweetest ‘Babbo’ mine!” she dictated in one letter. “This is the reason that all the subjects are corrupted by impurity and iniquity.” A wound that is only covered with ointment, she warned him, and never burned or cut when it needs to be, “infects everything.” And she told him to be brave: “Be manly in my sight, and not timorous.” Above all, she wanted him back in Rome.

“Come, come, come, and do not wait for time, since time does not wait for you.”

— Catherine to Pope Gregory XI, 1376, Tommaseo no. CCVI (Scudder’s English, 1905)

Then, she wrote, he would be like the slain Lamb, who “without weapons in His hand slew our foes, coming in gentleness.” Florence, governed in those months by a council called the Eight of War, was in open conflict with the pope, and Catherine set out for Avignon to make peace between them. On 18 June 1376 she arrived at Avignon, a dyer’s daughter from Siena among the cardinals of the papal court. Two days later Gregory received her, with Raymond as her interpreter.

Her mission soon went wrong. When Florence’s own ambassadors reached Avignon, they disowned her and her mediation. Catherine wrote to the Eight in their own city. “Dearest fathers and brothers in Christ Jesus,” she began, “… with desire to see you true sons, humble and obedient to your father.” She had been received kindly at the court, she told them; they must not make her out to be a liar. And she scolded them for taxing the clergy.

At court she did not soften her message. In one of her early audiences she spoke against the vices of the papal court itself, and Gregory listened in silence. Some of the prelates were less patient. Three of them came to question her, hoping to catch her in heresy. They failed, and the pope’s physician, Francesco Casini, told her disciple Stefano Maconi afterward: “If they had not found this virgin Catherine had a solid foundation, she would never have made a more unfortunate voyage.” Elys de Turenne, the wife of the pope’s nephew, tested her in a crueler way. While Catherine was rapt in prayer, Elys stabbed her feet with a needle. Catherine felt nothing until she came back to herself, and then she felt the pain.

The decisive moment came when Gregory asked her to tell him the will of God about his return to Rome. At first she refused: “It is not meet that a wretched little woman should give advice to the Sovereign Pontiff.” Then she answered him with a question. “Who knoweth this better than your Holiness,” she said, “who vowed to God that you would do this thing?” Gregory was astonished. He had made that vow in secret, at the conclave that elected him, and he had told no one.

Back in Siena, her mother was anxious about her. Catherine wrote to her from Avignon with great tenderness, and pointed her to the Virgin Mary, who had let the disciples go.

“With desire have I desired to see you a true mother, not only of my body but of my soul.”

— Catherine to her mother, Lapa, from Avignon, 1376, Tommaseo no. CCXL (Scudder’s English, 1905)

“I want you to learn from her, dearest mother,” Catherine wrote. In another letter she encouraged the pope. It would seem to him, she wrote, that he stood like a lamb among wolves, but he must take heart and not fear. “Up, father, carry out the resolution you have made about your coming.” Catherine left Avignon before him. She passed through Marseilles and was in Genoa by early October. On 29 October 1376 Gregory set sail, and on 17 January 1377 he entered Rome. The vow that no one knew had been kept.

“Our New Christ on Earth”

Catherine came home to Siena. It was probably now, in 1377, that she waited for Niccolò di Toldo at the block. Caffarini, who stood in the crowd, added that Christ received the young man’s blood and his soul, and that the soul turned back and bowed to her in thanks. That spring and summer she went out with a band of her disciples to Rocca d’Orcia, among the Salimbeni, on missions of peace. On the Thursday of Holy Week she wrote to the prisoners of Gaddo Accorimboni, the podestà of Gubbio. The silent girl of the cell now lived among quarrels, prisons, and roads.

On 27 March 1378 Gregory XI died in Rome, and the cardinals met to elect his successor while the Roman crowd outside shouted for “a Roman, a Roman!” In the confusion the aged Cardinal Tebaldeschi was dressed in the papal robes and set on the throne by mistake, and while the people kissed his feet, the old man raved about antipopes. The man the cardinals had actually chosen was the Archbishop of Bari, who took the name Urban VI.

The Prior of Gorgona wrote to Catherine that “our new Christ on earth is a terrible man.” She wrote to Urban anyway, as she had written to Gregory, and urged him to show charity to those under him. “Oh me, sweet my Babbo, bring us a remedy!” she wrote. “And give refreshment to the desperate desires of the servants of God, who die and cannot die.”

That summer she was in Florence when the city exploded. On 20 July 1378 the Ciompi rose in revolt, and for three days Florence was in turmoil. Catherine’s own life was in danger from the mob, and still she would not leave. She stayed in Florence until the treaty was signed, and only about 2 August did she go, leaving behind a farewell letter to the government of the city.

“You have the desire of reforming your city; but I tell you that this desire will never be fulfilled, unless you strive to throw to the ground the hatred and rancour of your hearts.”

— Catherine to the Signoria of Florence, August 1378 (Gardner’s English, 1907)

She went home to Siena, and there, in the late summer, she began to dictate a book.

A Bridge Over the Stormy River

According to Raymond, she dictated it in ecstasy, while her secretaries wrote down her words. It is called the Dialogue, or in Italian the Libro della divina dottrina, the Book of Divine Doctrine, and it is written as a conversation between God and a soul. The soul asks; God answers. In the last letter she wrote, Catherine called it simply “the book in which I found some recreation.” By the early autumn of 1378 the work was done: an introduction and treatises on discretion, prayer, tears, divine providence, and obedience.

The book opens with a soul that lifts herself up, “athirst with very great desire for the honour of God and the salvation of souls.” And the soul stays in a room. She remains, the book says, “in the cell of self-knowledge, in order to know better the goodness of God towards her.” The cell her family had tried to take from her as a girl had become the first lesson of her teaching. She had resolved then never to leave it, and she had carried it to Pisa, to Avignon, and through the streets of Florence.

From that cell the soul looks out at the world, and God shows her the way across it. The image she gave for that way is a bridge. Human life is a river, a stormy sea, and God has built a bridge over it, which is his Son.

“I gave you the bridge of my Son, so that crossing the river you would not drown. That river is the stormy sea of this dark life.”

— God to the soul, Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, ch. XXI (the same number in Thorold’s English and the Italian; our translation)

The old sentence from her years of silence returns in the book in new words. God tells her that he is “He who is, and they are they who are not,” and late in the book the soul answers him in her own voice: “I am she who is not.” The girl who had heard that truth alone in her cell now handed it on to anyone who would read.

While she dictated, the Church was splitting in two. On 20 September 1378 cardinals meeting at Fondi elected another pope, who took the name Clement VII. Now there were two men claiming the chair of Peter.

Fire in All Italy

Before the election she had written to the Count of Fondi. Now she gave herself to the cause of Urban VI, whom she held to be the true pope, and that autumn Urban called her to Rome.

In 1378 she wrote to Queen Giovanna of Naples as she wrote to everyone else, beginning “Dearest mother in sweet Christ Jesus.” In another letter to the queen that year she wrote: “Drown yourself a little in the blood of Christ crucified. There let the cloud of self-love dissolve, and servile fear, and the poison of hatred and of your own disdain.”

The same year she wrote to Stefano Maconi, one of her disciples, who was in Siena. The letter concerned Pope Urban and a company there called the Company of the Virgin Mary. One sentence of that letter has traveled around the world, usually in a form she never used.

“If you are what you ought to be, you will set fire to all Italy, and not only yonder.”

— Catherine to Stefano Maconi, 1378, Tommaseo no. CCCLXVIII (Scudder’s English, 1905)

“Yonder” was Siena, where Stefano was. Her own fire was burning down fast. In a letter of her last months she offered herself for the divided Church: “O eternal God, receive the sacrifice of my life in … this mystical body of Holy Church.”

A few days before the end, her disciple Bartolommeo di Domenico, who was about to leave Rome, asked for a sign. The next day she seemed well. On the day he left, she fell ill again, and he did not see her alive again.

The Last Morning in Rome

The last morning was Sunday, 29 April 1380, the Sunday before the Ascension. Before dawn her spiritual family gathered around her bed in Rome. Giovanni Tantucci gave her absolution, and the Abbot of Sant’Antimo anointed her. What followed is known from a letter that her disciple Barduccio Canigiani wrote to a nun, Suor Caterina Petribuoni.

For two hours she struggled as if she were being attacked by demons. Those around her heard her say, “Peccavi, Domine, miserere mei,” I have sinned, Lord, have mercy on me, and “Credo, credo,” I believe, I believe. At one moment she seemed to answer an accuser whom no one else could see: “Never vainglory, but always the true glory and praise of Jesus Christ crucified.”

Then the struggle ended, and her face changed. She sat up, leaning on Alessa Saracini, the friend who had been with her since the early days in Siena. Before them all she made a general confession, accusing herself of negligence toward souls and toward the Church. Then she spoke to each of her spiritual children in turn and gave each of them a task. To Stefano Maconi she said he must obey and go to the Carthusians, and he did.

Lapa was there. The mother who had fought her daughter’s vocation, who had taken her to the baths at Vignone and worried over her at Avignon, now asked her dying daughter for her blessing. Of those hours Barduccio wrote: “verily, I tell you it was a sweet sorrow.” Catherine told her children, as Raymond later recorded it, that she had given her life for the Church. She prayed for Urban VI as the true Sovereign Pontiff.

“Father, into Thy hands I commend my soul and my spirit.”

— Catherine’s last words, from Barduccio Canigiani’s letter, 1380 (Gardner’s English, 1907)

Before the end she cried out many times the word that stood at the head of so many of her letters: “Blood, blood.” She died about midday. Raymond says she was thirty-three.

A Head Carried Home to Siena

On that same Sunday, far away in Genoa, Raymond of Capua was packing his bundle to travel. He stopped before an image of the Virgin to say a Hail Mary. As he prayed, he heard a voice within him: “Fear not, I am here for your sake; I am in heaven for you.” He did not yet know that she had died.

In Rome, Stefano Maconi carried her body to the Dominican church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. It lay there until the evening of Tuesday, 1 May, and the crowds would not stay away. Cardinals and common people pressed in to touch her, and they tore pieces from her clothes to keep. Many sick people, it was reported, were cured in the church before she was buried. Giovanni Tantucci tried to preach in her honor, but the noise of the crowd drowned him out. The woman who had once said that the world would stone her if it knew her now had Rome at her feet. Pope Urban VI paid for her funeral, and the Senator of Rome, Giovanni Cenci, held another. Stefano laid her in a coffin of cypress wood in the friars’ cemetery, and kissed her.

Her friends kept what they could of her. Stefano took one of her teeth, and Alessa and Neri di Landoccio were given others. Raymond tells what happened when a young man in Rome named Nicolò, called Cola, the stepson of Cincio Tancancini, lay dying of an abscess in his throat. Alessa held Catherine’s tooth to his throat, and the abscess burst, as if a stone had fallen from it, and he recovered. Raymond saw the young man himself, and the physician, Master Jacopo di Santa Maria Rotonda, told him the story. In a letter of 22 May, her disciple Nigi di Doccio remembered that she had told them she would be more useful to them dead than living.

In October 1381 Raymond opened her grave and moved her body to a tomb of stone, a move she had once foretold to him. Then, with Urban’s permission, he separated her head from her body and sent it secretly to Siena with two friars. One of them was Tommaso della Fonte, the relative who had told her as a girl to cut off her hair. For years the head waited in a sacristy chest, and Raymond did not honor it openly. Then, on a Thursday, 5 May, sometime in the later 1380s, Siena received it in a great procession, with children dressed in white and carrying roses, and all the bells ringing. That night, Raymond remembered, the friars sat down to supper with bread enough for five, and fifty were fed. He was there.

Raymond had begun to write her life in 1385, at the request of her spiritual sons and daughters in Siena, and he finished it in 1391. He wrote it to bring about her canonization. The cause moved slowly. On 3 May 1411, in Venice, the Dominican inquisitor Bartolomeo of Ferrara preached a sermon mostly in her praise, and the congregation murmured. Tommaso Caffarini, who had stood in the crowd at Toldo’s execution, preached next, and a complaint went to the bishop, Francesco Bembo. The bishop opened an inquiry into whether the friars had honored her publicly before the Church allowed it, and from 1412 to 1416 witnesses gave their testimony under oath. The friars were cleared, and the sworn testimony waited for its day.

That day came with a Sienese pope. Enea Silvio Piccolomini, who took the name Pius II, decided on the canonization during a stay in Siena in 1459, and on 29 June 1461 he declared her a saint in St. Peter’s. He wrote the bull and the prayers of her feast himself, and the hymn he composed for her named the wounds of Christ she bore, though the bull did not. Paul VI would quote one sentence of the bull five centuries later. No one ever came to her, it says, who did not go away wiser and better; her learning was infused, not acquired, and she seemed a teacher before she was a pupil. The painter Pinturicchio later put the scene on the walls of the Piccolomini Library in Siena cathedral.

Her head was set in a silver bust in 1468. When fire broke out in San Domenico on 3 December 1531, a Florentine lay brother named Anselm, his clothes soaked with water, rushed into the burning church and carried it out, damaged but saved.

A Teacher Before a Pupil

The honors came slowly over the centuries that followed. Pope Urban VIII approved her stigmata by his own authority, ruling that they were marks of light and not of blood. He also moved her feast to 30 April, because the day of her death already belonged to St. Peter Martyr. In troubled times, Pius IX placed the See of Peter itself under her protection. On 18 June 1939 Pope Pius XII named her and Francis of Assisi the principal patrons of Italy. He called her a most strong and devout virgin, the glory and the defense of her country and of her faith.

Then came the title no woman had ever held. In December 1966 a Vatican session took up the question of whether a woman could be named a Doctor of the Church, and in 1968 Paul VI confirmed that one could. At the request of the Master of the Dominican order, Aniceto Fernández, and many cardinals and bishops, the case for Catherine was examined and approved. In October 1970, during Mass in St. Peter’s, Paul VI declared “Saint Catherine, virgin of Siena,” a Doctor of the universal Church. Her title rested, he said, on her holiness and on the special excellence of her teaching, a wisdom infused by God. On 1 October 1999 Pope John Paul II named her a co-patroness of Europe, with Bridget of Sweden and Teresa Benedicta of the Cross, and remembered the inner cell she had built as a girl.

In 1961 Pope John XXIII invited all the faithful to keep the fifth centenary of her canonization. Today the Catholic Church keeps her feast on 29 April, the day she died. Her body, laid in a carved sarcophagus in 1430 by Antoninus, the prior of the Minerva, has rested since 1855 beneath the high altar of the Minerva in Rome. Her head is in Siena, in San Domenico, the church above which a six-year-old girl, standing in a lane, once saw Christ enthroned and dressed as a pope.

She had wanted nothing but a cell, and she had been sent into the noise of the world, to plague wards, to a scaffold, to two popes and a Church torn in half. She never found a way back to the silent room of her girlhood, and she never needed one. The cell went with her, and the God she met there kept sending her out to souls. In the last pages of her book, dictated between a riot and a schism, she turned from all of it to him.

“Thou, oh eternal Trinity, art a deep Sea, into which the deeper I enter the more I find, and the more I find the more I seek.”

— Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, closing prayer, Thorold’s ch. CXLVIII (Italian ch. CLXVII), translated by Algar Thorold, 1896

A Note on the Sources

Most of what is known about Catherine comes from people who loved her. Raymond of Capua wrote his Latin Legenda Maior between 1385 and 1391 to win her canonization; Tommaso Caffarini wrote the Italian Legenda minore; Barduccio Canigiani described her death in a letter. An anonymous Florentine wrote the Miracoli in 1374, independently of Raymond. Her own words come from her letters, in Niccolò Tommaseo’s Italian edition of 1860, and from the Dialogue. Raymond’s words to and about her are quoted here in Edmund Gardner’s English of 1907. The words on the heart and the stigmata are translated here from Raymond’s Latin. Her words on the pain at Pisa come from the old English version of his life printed by Augusta Drane. In Algar Thorold’s English of the Dialogue, the chapter numbers match the Italian until about chapter CXXXV and differ after it, so both numbers are given for the closing prayer.

Several points are disputed. Caffarini gives her birth year as 1347. Raymond gives no year, only her age of thirty-three at death, and the historian Robert Fawtier suspected that number because it is Christ’s age. The Miracoli even contain a second chronology that would place her birth about 1355. Raymond says Lapa bore twenty-five children and that Catherine was not the last, while Caffarini says she was the last. The often repeated claim that she was the twenty-third or twenty-fourth child was not found in any source read for this life. The story that the Mantellate refused her as a young girl comes from Raymond alone, and Fawtier noted that their rule set no such condition and that married women and girls appear on their lists. In the Miracoli her espousal is told differently: there Christ gave her the ring on the night after she drank from the sore of the sick sister. Her stigmata were invisible in her lifetime. Paul VI described them with the words “if Raymond is believed,” Barduccio’s letter on her death never mentions them, and Caffarini defended them at length. The later quarrel over them between Franciscans and Dominicans, and any decree of Sixtus IV about it, were not read.

Tommaseo did not know the year of Niccolò di Toldo’s execution, and Gardner dates it to 1377. Raymond names the young man cured with her tooth as Cincio Tancancini’s stepson, though Drane writes that it was Cincio himself; Raymond is followed here. Drane dates Urban VIII’s move of her feast to 1630, and Wikipedia to 1628. Paul VI’s apostolic letter declaring her a Doctor is dated Sunday, 4 October 1970, while the Vatican’s page for his homily at the proclamation is headed 3 October. That Pius IX named her a co-patron of Rome by a decree of 1866, and that her feast returned to 29 April in the calendar reform of 1969, rest here only on Wikipedia. No source read calls her head incorrupt; Drane mentions only a nineteenth-century report praising the face.

The saying “Be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire” was not found in her letters or the Dialogue. It seems to be a loose modern paraphrase of her letter to Stefano Maconi, Tommaseo no. CCCLXVIII: “Se sarete quello che dovete essere, metterete fuoco in tutta Italia, non tanto costì.” If you are what you should be, you will set fire to all Italy, not only there.

How This Life Was Researched

This life was written from fifteen works in Italian, Latin, English, and French. Catherine’s own words were read in Italian, in Tommaseo’s edition of her letters and the 1928 text of the Dialogue, and checked against the public-domain English of Vida Scudder (1905) and Algar Thorold (1896). The research gathered thirteen passages of her own words with their Italian. Raymond’s life was read in the Latin of the Acta Sanctorum and through Gardner’s English, and Caffarini’s Legenda minore in Italian. Beside them stand Fawtier’s critical study of the sources, in French, and four papal documents from 1939 to 1999. The research marked sixteen details as new or seldom told in popular English accounts. Among them are her brother Stefano at the childhood vision, the girl with one loaf of bread, her examination at Florence in 1374, and the sermon at Venice that began the inquiry into her life. Several sources were not read. Among them are the sworn depositions of the Venice inquiry, known here only through Gardner and Drane, the text of Pius II’s bull, the 1969 calendar, and Raymond’s own text on her “mystic death” of 1370. Nor were the Italian of Barduccio’s letter, the first two volumes of Tommaseo, the modern editions of Laurent, Misciattelli, and Dupré Theseider, or any document on the stigmata dispute. The popular patronages of nurses, of protection against fire, and of women who suffer miscarriage were found only in a Wikipedia list, with no source, and are not given here.

saint.relic_description:
Catherine died in Rome on 29 April 1380. Stefano Maconi carried her body to Santa Maria sopra Minerva, where it lay until the evening of 1 May; she was buried in a cypress coffin in the friars’ cemetery. In October 1381 Raymond of Capua moved the body to a stone tomb and, with Urban VI’s permission, separated the head and sent it secretly to Siena. In 1430 Antoninus, prior of the Minerva, placed the body in a carved sarcophagus with a wooden effigy. In 1487 the right hand went to SS. Domenico e Sisto in Rome and a foot to SS. Giovanni e Paolo in Venice. On 17 April 1855 the Master General Jandel opened the sarcophagus; the tomb was set beneath the high altar, which Pius IX consecrated on 4 August 1855.

The head was received in Siena in procession on a 5 May in the later 1380s and is kept in San Domenico. It was set in a silver bust in 1468, saved from fire on 3 December 1531 by a Florentine lay brother, Anselm, and placed in a crystal reliquary in the nineteenth century; the thumb of the right hand was carried before the silver bust in the annual procession. Drane cites a nineteenth-century report that praised the face; no source read calls the head incorrupt.

Other relics named by Drane, after Gigli: part of a habit at San Nicola in Carcere, a discipline and chain at Santa Cecilia, and a white shoe at Santa Maddalena, all in Rome; her teeth went to Stefano Maconi, Alessa Saracini, and Neri di Landoccio. The painted crucifix of Giunta Pisano, before which she received the stigmata at Pisa in 1375, was carried to Siena by night in 1563.
saint.relic_location: Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome (body); San Domenico, Siena (head)

miracles.miracles:
This list gathers the visions, healings, and other wonders attributed to St. Catherine of Siena, with their sources and their status. Most come from people who knew her: her confessor Raymond of Capua, whose Latin life (finished in 1391) was written for her canonization; Tommaso Caffarini, whose Italian Legenda minore followed; the anonymous Florentine Miracoli, written in 1374 while she was alive; and witnesses heard at the Venice inquiry of 1411 to 1416. Each account says which source tells it and gives its status: recognized by the Church, reported by Raymond or a sworn witness, reported by a later writer, legendary, or contested. Only the stigmata are marked as recognized by the Church, because a papal document says so. The bull of canonization of 1461 was not read for this page, so any miracles it approves are not identified here. The list makes no claim of scientific proof, and it does not dismiss any account.

Recognized by the Church

The invisible stigmata at Santa Cristina, Pisa, 1375

On the fourth Sunday of Lent, 1 April 1375, after Raymond of Capua’s Mass in the church of Santa Cristina at Pisa, Catherine knelt, rose on her knees with her arms stretched out, and fell as if mortally wounded. She told Raymond that she now carried the stigmata of the Lord Jesus in her body. She had seen five blood-red rays come from the wounds of the crucified Christ toward her hands, feet, and heart; she begged that no marks should show, and the rays reached her as pure light. She told him the pain in the five places was so great that she could not live without a new miracle, and a week later, after Communion in the same church, the pain was eased.

No wound was seen on her in life. Pope Urban VIII approved her stigmata by his own authority, according to Paul VI, and Drane writes that he ruled them luminous, not bloody. Pius II’s hymn for her feast names them, though his bull of canonization does not. Paul VI, telling the story in 1970, added the words “if Raymond is believed.” Barduccio Canigiani’s letter on her death never mentions them, and Caffarini wrote a long defense of them. The later dispute between Franciscans and Dominicans, and any decree of Sixtus IV, were not read.

Status: recognized by the Church (Urban VIII); also contested.

Source: Raymond of Capua, Legenda Maior §195, Acta Sanctorum April III, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Caffarini, Legenda minore, ed. Grottanelli, p. 77, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft; Drane, vol. 1, pp. 307–311, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft; Paul VI, Mirabilis in Ecclesia Deus §2 and §4, https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/la/apost_letters/documents/hf_p-vi_apl_19701004_mirabilis-in-ecclesia.html.

During Catherine’s life

Christ enthroned over San Domenico, about 1353

When Catherine was about six, walking home along Vallepiatta in Siena with her brother Stefano, she saw Christ seated on a throne in the air above the church of the Dominican friars, dressed as a pope, with the apostles Peter, Paul, and John. He blessed her, and Stefano pulled her hand to bring her back. Caffarini’s version has the apostles but does not mention Stefano or the tiara.

Status: a vision reported by Raymond and by Caffarini.

Source: Gardner, p. 8 (from Raymond), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog; Caffarini, Legenda minore, p. 11, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft.

Carried down the stairs as a child

As a small child Catherine would kneel on every stair of her house to greet the Virgin Mary. Caffarini adds that she seemed to be carried visibly through the air down the stairs without touching the steps.

Status: legendary; told by Caffarini only.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, p. 11, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft; Gardner, p. 8, https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

The girl with one loaf, lifted in a cave

At about six or seven, with one loaf of bread in her dress, Catherine left Siena for “the desert of the holy Fathers.” She found a cave or cellar outside the walls, was lifted from the ground in prayer until the ninth hour, understood that this was not God’s will, and found herself back at the city gate. She told no one, and her mother thought she had been at her sister Bonaventura’s house.

Status: legendary in character; told by Caffarini only.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, pp. 11–12, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft.

The white dove over her head

When her family opposed her vocation, her father, Jacomo, found her praying in her brother Stefano’s room with a white dove above her head. After that he let her serve God freely.

Status: reported by Raymond.

Source: Gardner, p. 11 (from Raymond), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

Learning to read without a teacher

During her three years of silence in her cell, Raymond says, Catherine learned to read miraculously.

Status: reported by Raymond.

Source: Gardner, p. 22 (from Raymond), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

Living without food

Raymond wrote that in the years when he was a witness of her life she lived without food or drink as nourishment, and that physicians brought to her admitted it was beyond nature; he warned readers not to copy her. Her confessor had once ordered her to eat, and she chewed the food and spat it out. Critics in her lifetime, including men respected in the spiritual life, said she did not fast but ate very well in secret.

Status: reported by Raymond; contested in her lifetime.

Source: Raymond, Legenda Maior §§58–60 and §172, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Gardner, pp. 9, 12–13, https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

Fifty-five days on Communion alone, 1373

From the autumn of 1372 eating grew harder for her for eight months. In 1373, from Passion Sunday to the Ascension, she is said to have taken nothing but Holy Communion for fifty-five days; Bartolommeo di Domenico gave an account of the eve of the Ascension. Caffarini adds that on the Rogation days an angel brought her the Host in a veil.

Status: reported by her companions; the angel is legendary.

Source: Drane, vol. 1, pp. 201–203, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft.

“I was in thy heart”

Near the end of her three years of silence, Raymond writes, Catherine suffered an assault by demons. When it ended, Christ showed himself to her on the cross and told her, “I was in thy heart.”

Status: a vision reported by Raymond.

Source: Gardner, pp. 20–21 (from Raymond), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

The espousal ring, probably 1366

On the last day of carnival, probably in 1366, Christ took Catherine as his bride. In Raymond’s account the Virgin Mary held out Catherine’s hand, King David played a psaltery, and Christ gave her a ring of gold with four pearls and a diamond, which she alone could see. The Florentine Miracoli of 1374 tell it differently: she received a ring on the night after she drank from a sick sister’s sore (see below). Paul VI named the mystical espousal among her graces in 1970, and John Paul II placed it when she was twenty.

Status: reported by Raymond; the details are contested between the sources.

Source: Gardner, pp. 24–26 (Raymond, Legenda I.xii §115), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog; Fawtier, p. 95, https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt; Paul VI, homily, October 1970, https://www.vatican.va/content/paul-vi/it/homilies/1970/documents/hf_p-vi_hom_19701003.html.

Pricked with needles in ecstasy, Siena and Avignon

In Siena, while Catherine was rapt in prayer, she was thrown out of a church, a friar kicked her, and another pricked her with a needle; she felt the pain only when she came to herself. At Avignon in 1376 Elys de Turenne, the wife of the pope’s nephew, stabbed her feet with a needle during an ecstasy, and again she felt it only afterward.

Status: reported by Raymond and by Simone da Cortona at the Venice inquiry (known here through Gardner); the source of the Avignon story was not seen.

Source: Gardner, pp. 50–51 and 184, https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

The exchange of hearts, July 1370

In July 1370, after Communion, Catherine felt Christ open her side and take her heart. She told her confessor she had no heart, and he laughed; she insisted she lived without one. Two days later, alone in the Dominican chapel in Siena, she saw Christ in light with a red, shining heart, and he told her he was giving her his heart so that she might always live by it. Raymond says a scar remained, which her companions told him and many others they had seen, and which she confirmed when he asked. Tommaso della Fonte dates the event to 20 July 1370.

Status: reported by Raymond; named in Pius II’s poem for her feast; not defined by the Church.

Source: Raymond, Legenda Maior §§179–180, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Drane, vol. 1, p. 109, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft; Drane, vol. 2, p. 343, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

The “mystic death,” 1370

In 1370, Gardner writes, summarizing Raymond, Catherine lay as if dead for about four hours on a Sunday. Bartolommeo di Domenico testified that he was preaching in San Domenico when the rumor of her death came, that her cell was full of people, and that she revived before him. Raymond’s own text on this event was not read for this page.

Status: reported by Raymond and by a witness at the Venice inquiry, known here only through Gardner; named in Pius II’s poem.

Source: Gardner, pp. 82–84 (Processus coll. 1332–1333), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog; Drane, vol. 2, p. 343, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

An invisible nail in her right hand

Before the stigmata at Pisa, Raymond writes, Christ offered Catherine a nail and pressed it into her right palm. She told Raymond that she already had his stigmata in her right hand: invisible, but felt and always painful. Fawtier notes that Raymond took this from Tommaso della Fonte’s notes, and that the Miracoli do not know it.

Status: reported by Raymond; the source chain is questioned by Fawtier.

Source: Raymond, Legenda Maior §§192–193, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Fawtier, chapter on the birth date, https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt.

Drinking from a sick sister’s sore

A sister who had slandered Catherine fell ill with a cancer, and Catherine nursed her. Sickened by the smell while dressing the sore, she told her own body that it would take in what so displeased it, and drank the matter from the bowl; she said afterward that she had never tasted so perfect a drink. That night, Caffarini writes, Christ put her mouth to his side and said, “Drink, most loving daughter, from my side.” The Miracoli of 1374 tell a form of the story and place a ring espousal that night.

Status: devotional legend; told by Caffarini and the Miracoli.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, pp. 62–63, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft; Fawtier, p. 95, https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt.

The cask of wine that did not run dry

A cask of wine went on giving wine, the story says, long after it should have been empty. When people began to talk about it, Catherine begged God to turn the wine to dregs so that the talk would stop, and the wine turned to sediment.

Status: reported by Raymond and by the Miracoli.

Source: Drane, vol. 1, p. 306 (Raymond, part II, ch. ii), https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft; Fawtier, p. 94 (Miracoli §24), https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt.

Christ as a beggar

The Florentine Miracoli tell that Catherine gave her tunic to a beggar who was Christ.

Status: reported by the Miracoli (1374).

Source: Fawtier, p. 94 (Miracoli §23), https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt.

The foot of St. Agnes at Montepulciano

At Montepulciano Catherine bent to kiss the foot of St. Agnes, and the foot rose to her lips.

Status: reported by the Miracoli and by Raymond.

Source: Fawtier, p. 94 (Miracoli §22; Raymond §326), https://archive.org/details/saintecatherined01fawt.

Matteo di Cenni rises from the plague, Siena, 1374

Matteo di Cenni, rector of the Misericordia hospital in Siena, fell sick with plague in the night, and a physician found the evident signs of the pestilence. Raymond pleaded with Catherine; she asked whether he took her for a God, then smiled and promised. From the street she called, “Rise, Master Matthew, rise; this is no time to lie softly in bed,” and the fever and the swelling in his groin left at once. That morning they ate raw onions together. Caffarini’s Legenda minore dates it to 1373 and the Miracoli to 1374 (the Sienese year began in March).

Status: reported by Raymond, who was there.

Source: Raymond, Legenda Maior part II §§24–25, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Drane, vol. 1, pp. 225–227, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft.

Fra Santi held back from death, 1374

The hermit Fra Santi, taken to the Misericordia with plague, was nursed by Catherine. Caffarini gives her command to him: “I command you, blessed soul … not to pass away now.” He recovered.

Status: reported by Caffarini and the Miracoli; Fra Santi’s own testimony is cited but was not read.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, pp. 105–106, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft; Drane, vol. 1, pp. 227–228, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft.

Raymond’s own recovery from plague, 1374

Caffarini names Raymond of Capua as one of those who caught the plague in 1374 and recovered through Catherine’s prayer. The Miracoli speak only of a religious in her service. Raymond’s own account was not read.

Status: reported by Caffarini; the name needs checking against Raymond.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, pp. 106–107, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft.

The tempted monk of Gorgona, 1375

On the island of Gorgona, where she saw the sea for the first time, a young Carthusian was tempted to take his own life. Catherine’s mantle touched him, and the temptation left him. The prior, Bartolommeo Serafini, also told of monks saved from a storm.

Status: reported by the prior of Gorgona.

Source: Gardner, p. 135, https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

The pope’s secret vow named, Avignon, 1376

When Gregory XI asked Catherine at Avignon to tell him the will of God about returning to Rome, she answered, “Who knoweth this better than your Holiness, who vowed to God that you would do this thing?” Gregory was amazed, because he had made the vow in secret at the conclave and told no one.

Status: reported by Raymond, who interpreted at her audiences.

Source: Gardner, pp. 182–183 (Raymond, Legenda II.iv.7), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

Niccolò di Toldo’s soul, Siena, about 1377

Catherine received the head of the executed Niccolò di Toldo in her hands. Caffarini, who was present, adds that Christ received the young man’s blood and soul, and that the soul turned back and bowed to her in thanks. Catherine herself wrote that in the crowd she saw no one.

Status: a vision reported by Caffarini.

Source: Caffarini, Legenda minore, pp. 94–95, https://archive.org/details/leggendaminoredi00grotuoft; Catherine, letter CCLXXIII, Tommaseo, vol. 4, https://archive.org/details/lettereconproemi04cathuoft.

A sign for Bartolommeo, Rome, 1380

A few days before her death, Bartolommeo di Domenico asked for a sign before leaving Rome. The next day she was well; on the day he left, she fell ill again.

Status: reported by Bartolommeo at the Venice inquiry, known here through Gardner.

Source: Gardner, pp. 348–349 (Processus coll. 1358–1361), https://archive.org/details/saintcatherines00gardgoog.

After Catherine’s death

A voice at Genoa, 29 April 1380

On the day she died, Raymond of Capua was at Genoa, packing to travel. As he said a Hail Mary before an image of the Virgin, he heard an interior voice: “Fear not, I am here for your sake; I am in heaven for you.”

Status: reported by Raymond about himself.

Source: Drane, vol. 2, pp. 277–278, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

Cures at the Minerva before her burial, 1380

While her body lay in Santa Maria sopra Minerva in Rome until the evening of 1 May 1380, crowds touched it and tore pieces of her clothes, and many sick people were reported cured in the church.

Status: reported in the early accounts summarized by Drane.

Source: Drane, vol. 2, p. 276, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

Thomas Petra’s vision, 1380

About thirty days after her death, Tommaso Petra saw a procession in white. The account is in the second deposition of Bartolommeo di Domenico.

Status: reported at second hand at the Venice inquiry, known here through Drane.

Source: Drane, vol. 2, pp. 278–279, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

Five marks seen at her wake

Prior Antonio of Siena claimed in a letter to Raymond that he saw five marks on her body at her wake; the letter is known through Lombardelli and Drane. Relics of a foot in Venice and a hand in Rome are said to show the stigma, and Drane mentions a photograph showing a spot in the palm where light shines through.

Status: reported at third hand; contested, since no mark was seen in her life.

Source: Drane, vol. 1, p. 311, https://archive.org/details/historystcatheri01dranuoft.

Her tooth and the young man Cola, Rome

A young man of Rome, Nicolò, called Cola, the stepson of Cincio Tancancini, lay dying of quinsy. Alessa Saracini held one of Catherine’s teeth to his throat; the abscess burst, as if a stone had fallen, and he recovered. Raymond saw the young man himself, and the physician, Master Jacopo di Santa Maria Rotonda, told him the story. Drane says Cincio himself was healed; Raymond’s text says the stepson.

Status: reported by Raymond.

Source: Raymond, Legenda Maior part III §392, https://archive.org/details/actasanctorum12unse; Drane, vol. 2, p. 277, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

The translation she foretold, 1381

In October 1381 Raymond opened her grave in the friars’ cemetery at the Minerva and moved her body to a stone tomb. Catherine had foretold this move to him at Voragine, on the eve of St. Francis.

Status: reported by Raymond (as given by Drane).

Source: Drane, vol. 2, pp. 282–283, https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

Bread for five feeds fifty, Siena

On the day Siena received her head in procession, sometime in the later 1380s, the friars of San Domenico had bread enough for five at their table that night, and it fed fifty. Raymond was present.

Status: reported by Raymond, who was there.

Source: Drane, vol. 2, pp. 289–290 (Raymond, part II, ch. 11), https://archive.org/details/historyofstcathe02dranuoft.

teachings.teachings:
Catherine of Siena dictated many letters to her disciples and one book, the Dialogue, at Siena in the late summer and autumn of 1378. In 1970 Pope Paul VI declared her a Doctor of the Church, saying that the title rested on her holiness and on the special excellence of her teaching. The themes below give her own words with the letter or chapter, and a fact from her life that shows how she lived them. Her letters are cited by Tommaseo’s numbers (1860). For the Dialogue, Thorold’s English chapter numbers (1896) match the Italian until about chapter CXXXV and differ after it; both are given where they differ. Translations are our own unless Scudder, Thorold, or Gardner is named.

The cell of self-knowledge

Catherine taught that the soul must live in an inner cell, where it comes to know itself and, through that knowledge, the goodness of God. The Dialogue opens with the soul in that cell.

“remaining in the cell of self-knowledge, in order to know better the goodness of God towards her.”

— Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, ch. I (Thorold’s English, 1896)

She learned this as a girl. When her family took away her room and made her the servant of the house, she built a cell in her mind and resolved never to leave it.

She who is not, and He who is

At the center of her teaching is a contrast that, by Raymond’s account, Christ taught her in her years of silence: “Thou art she who art not, and I am He who am.” In the Dialogue God says, “I am He who is, and they are they who are not,” and the soul answers in her own voice.

“I am she who is not.”

— Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, ch. CXXXIV (the same number in Thorold’s English and the Italian)

Before Gregory XI at Avignon she first refused to advise him, calling herself a “wretched little woman,” and then reminded him of a vow he had made in secret.

Christ the Bridge

In the Dialogue God describes his Son as a bridge over a river, given so that those who cross it will not drown. The river is the stormy sea of this dark life.

“I gave you the bridge of my Son, so that crossing the river you would not drown. That river is the stormy sea of this dark life.”

— God to the soul, Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, ch. XXI (the same number in Thorold’s English and the Italian; our translation)

She dictated the book at Siena in 1378, weeks after a revolt in Florence had put her life in danger and while the Church was splitting between two popes.

The Blood of Christ

Catherine usually opened her letters by saying that she wrote “in His precious Blood.” In the Blood of Christ crucified, she told a queen, self-love, servile fear, and hatred dissolve.

“Drown yourself a little in the blood of Christ crucified. There let the cloud of self-love dissolve, and servile fear, and the poison of hatred and of your own disdain.”

— Catherine to Queen Giovanna of Naples, 1378, Tommaseo no. CCCXVII (our translation)

She told the condemned Niccolò di Toldo that he would go to his death “bathed in the sweet blood of the Son of God,” and as she died in Rome she cried out many times, “Blood, blood.”

Thirst for God and for souls

The Dialogue begins with a soul that rises toward God out of desire for the honor of God and the salvation of souls.

“When a soul lifts herself up, athirst with very great desire for the honour of God and the salvation of souls …”

— Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, opening (Gardner’s English, 1907)

In the plague of 1374 she and Raymond of Capua visited the wards every day, and she nursed the hermit Fra Santi herself.

Courage to heal the Church

Catherine called Pope Gregory XI “Babbo,” Daddy, and in the same letters she told him to be brave. A wound that is only covered with ointment, she warned him, and never burned or cut when it must be, infects everything. She urged him to return from Avignon to Rome.

“Come, come, come, and do not wait for time, since time does not wait for you.”

— Catherine to Pope Gregory XI, 1376, Tommaseo no. CCVI (Scudder’s English, 1905)

She went to Avignon herself in June 1376 and spoke against the vices of the papal court to the pope’s face. In January 1377 Gregory entered Rome.

Peace begins in the heart

Catherine worked for peace between cities, families, and the pope. She told the rulers of Florence that their reform would fail unless they first threw down the hatred in their own hearts.

“You have the desire of reforming your city; but I tell you that this desire will never be fulfilled, unless you strive to throw to the ground the hatred and rancour of your hearts.”

— Catherine to the Signoria of Florence, August 1378 (Gardner’s English, 1907)

She wrote it as she left Florence after the Ciompi revolt, having stayed in the city, with her life in danger from the mob, until the treaty was signed.

Be what you ought to be

In 1378 she told a disciple that if he became what he ought to be, his fire would spread far beyond his own city. The popular line “Be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire” is not found in her writings; this is the sentence behind it.

“If you are what you ought to be, you will set fire to all Italy, and not only yonder.”

— Catherine to Stefano Maconi, 1378, Tommaseo no. CCCLXVIII (Scudder’s English, 1905)

“Yonder” was Siena, where Stefano was. On her deathbed she told him to obey and go to the Carthusians, and he did.

God, a deep sea

Catherine ended the Dialogue with a prayer to the Trinity. In it, finding God does not end the search: the more she finds, the more she seeks.

“Thou, oh eternal Trinity, art a deep Sea, into which the deeper I enter the more I find, and the more I find the more I seek.”

— Catherine of Siena, Dialogue, closing prayer, Thorold’s ch. CXLVIII (Italian ch. CLXVII), Thorold’s English, 1896

In the same prayer she asks what more God could have given her than himself, and longs, as the hart longs for the spring, to leave “the prison of this dark body.” She died at Rome on 29 April 1380.

gaps: Length: 7,308 words by the lint count (14 story chapters plus the source note and research paragraph), 11 block quotes, below the tier A target of 8,000–10,000. The three notes files hold about 9,800 words; every usable scene was told, and the Rome years 1378–80 are thin in the notes. More length would need more research (Raymond’s Legenda in full, the Venice depositions, Tommaseo vols I–II), not padding.

Not read: the Venice (Castellan) Process depositions (known only through Gardner and Drane); the text of Pius II’s bull Misericordias Domini (Laurent pp. 521–530); the 1969 calendar text; Raymond’s text on the 1370 “mystic death”; the Italian of Barduccio’s letter; Tommaseo vols I–II; Laurent’s Fontes, Misciattelli, Dupré Theseider; the separate Prayers; any document on the Sixtus IV stigmata dispute. Lamb’s 1960 translation of Raymond was not used.

Disputes stated in the biography’s source note: birth year 1347 (Caffarini) against Fawtier’s doubts and the Miracoli’s second chronology; 25 children and not last (Raymond) against last child (Caffarini); “23rd or 24th child” not found; the Mantellate “too beautiful / widows only” story (Raymond only; Fawtier); espousal (Raymond’s carnival ring against the Miracoli ring after the pus episode); invisible stigmata; Toldo year (Tommaseo unknown, Gardner 1377); tooth cure of Cincio’s stepson (Raymond) against Cincio (Drane); Urban VIII feast move 1630 (Drane) or 1628 (Wikipedia); Doctor letter 4 Oct 1970 against homily page 3 Oct.

Wikipedia-only items, kept out of the fields or attributed: Pius IX co-patronage of Rome by a decree of 13 April 1866 (Paul VI confirms only that Pius IX placed the See of Peter under her protection); restoration of the feast to 29 April in 1969; patronage of nurses, fire, miscarriage, and others (not given anywhere on the page).

Misattribution: “Be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire” is not in Tommaseo vols III–IV, Scudder, or the Dialogue; the source of the idea is Tommaseo CCCLXVIII to Stefano Maconi, quoted with locator. Tommaseo vols I–II were not searched.

Quotations from Raymond are in Gardner’s 1907 English, except the heart (§180), the right-hand nail (§193), the Pisa words (§195), and the Matteo command (part II §24–25), which are our translations of the Acta Sanctorum Latin (OCR lightly corrected in the notes; check against the scan before print), and the Pisa pain and Matteo dialogue, from the old English Legend via Drane.

Italian is quoted only from the exact copies in the notes (Toldo letter CCLXXIII; Caffarini’s Legenda minore “in presenzia mia”) and, in the source note only, the Maconi sentence CCCLXVIII, which the task required.

Miracles: only the stigmata are marked recognized by the Church (Urban VIII, per Paul VI); the canonization bull was not read, so any miracles it approves are not identified. Raymond’s own plague recovery is named only by Caffarini and needs checking.

Common English name with title.
biography: All facts from the three notes files; one-witness and legendary accounts attributed in the text; disputes in A Note on the Sources.
birth_year: 1347 per Caffarini’s Legenda minore and Gardner; Fawtier doubts it (Raymond gives only age 33 at death; the Miracoli contain a chronology pointing to about 1355).
death_year: 29 April 1380 (Paul VI, Mirabilis §2; Barduccio via Gardner).
feast_day_catholic: 29 April, her death day; Urban VIII moved it to 30 April (Drane); the return to 29 April in 1969 is from Wikipedia only (calendar text not read).
feast_day_orthodox: Western saint after 1054; no Orthodox commemoration in the notes.
categories: Holy_Women (laywoman, virgin), Ascetics (fasting, three years of silence), Miracle_Workers (reported miracles), Patron Saints (Italy 1939, Europe 1999). She was a Dominican tertiary living at home, not a nun.
patron: Italy (Pius XII brief, 1939); Europe (Spes aedificandi, 1999); See of Peter under her protection (Paul VI on Pius IX). Rome 1866 and popular patronages left out (Wikipedia only).
relic_description: Drane vol. 2 pp. 276–293; Gardner; Curtayne for the head in San Domenico. Incorrupt claim not made.
relic_location: Body at Santa Maria sopra Minerva, Rome; head in San Domenico, Siena (Drane; Curtayne; Paul VI for the Minerva).
miracles: 32 accounts, each with status and source; only the stigmata marked recognized by the Church.
teachings: Nine themes, each with her own words and a locator.
